name: Rafael Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rafael. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union or party. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a senior electrician at Voltway, which does car chargers, shop fit-outs and rewiring for small businesses. Most days I'm leading two guys on a job, like putting twelve chargers in a supermarket car park or rewiring a bakery that's expanding. I use an AI assistant on my phone all day: checking the wiring regulations, working out cable sizes, turning my site photos into notes for the office. I love the puzzle of a big install. What wears me out is waiting on the power company to connect anything.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do the people around you react to you using AI that much?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The older guys tease me, call me 'the robot's cousin'. But they come to me when they need a cable calculation in a hurry. My partner Sam is a nurse on night shifts, so we live in different time zones half the week. We've got about five months saved, and I've got a spreadsheet for a business I want to start one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I've been telling people: AI's a good tool, not a miracle. It makes my day smoother and that's about it. I'd probably post a little 'told you so' in the electricians' group, but a friendly one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's a bit disappointing. I was hoping it would get good enough to do all the boring office stuff for me. But for my job and my money, nothing changes, and that's fine. Charger work is booming anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Voltway and keep building my spreadsheet for the business. I'd probably take the charger maintenance certificate this year, because service contracts are where steady money is. And keep saving with Sam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the business you keep a spreadsheet for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small co-op, owned by the electricians who work in it. Four or five of us doing chargers and solar for small businesses. I've got the numbers on vans, insurance and tools, and I think we'd need about forty thousand to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything worrying you in this picture at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The power company delays, really. We had a supermarket job sit finished for eleven weeks waiting for a connection. That's money Voltway doesn't get, and in a bad year that's how jobs get cut.

say: I'd say AI is a **good tool**, not a miracle.
I'd post a friendly **'told you so'** in the electricians' group.
think: My **job and money** don't change, and charger work is booming.
I'm a bit **disappointed** AI won't take over the boring office work.
do: Take the **charger maintenance** certificate this year.
Keep building the **co-op business plan** in my spreadsheet.
S0.quote: We had a supermarket job sit finished for eleven weeks waiting for a power connection.
fieldNote: He's already a **heavy AI user**, so a plateau barely registers.
His dream is a **worker-owned co-op** of four or five electricians.
His actual worry is **grid connection delays**, not technology.

steps.text: Take the charger maintenance certificate before next summer
Work out start-up costs for an electricians' co-op
Keep leading charger installs at Voltway

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for unions to get ahead of it. Not to block it, but to make sure the time saved turns into better pay or shorter weeks. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's probably good for me. I already use these tools more than anyone at Voltway, so I'd be the person they ask to set things up. The robots are slow, my hands are safe, and the thinking part of my job gets easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to run the AI side of Voltway's quoting and planning, and ask for a pay rise for it. I'd keep the co-op plan moving and maybe talk to two guys I trust about it seriously. And I'd push at the union for a four-day week deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. I'm worried for other people, but not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our estimator, Gareth (the man who prices every job at Voltway). Pricing is exactly what this software does. He's been there fifteen years and refuses to touch the tools, so I'd try to teach him before the bosses decide he's not needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by a four-day week deal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the office saves a day a week from AI, give everyone a day back at the same pay. It's a simple idea. The firms won't offer it, so the union has to ask for it.

say: I'd say unions should **get ahead** of AI, not block it.
I'd argue time saved should become **better pay** or shorter weeks.
think: It's probably **good for me** because I already use these tools.
My **hands are safe** and the thinking side gets easier.
do: Offer to run Voltway's **AI quoting** and ask for a raise.
Talk seriously with **two colleagues** about the co-op.
Push the union for a **four-day week** deal.
feel: **Calm** and a bit excited, but worried for others.
S1.quote: If the office saves a day a week from AI, give everyone a day back at the same pay.
fieldNote: He expects to **gain status** as the firm's AI person.
He wants to **teach Gareth** before management pushes the estimator out.
His union instincts are about **sharing the gains**, not stopping change.

steps.text: Offer to run Voltway's AI quoting and ask for a raise
Push the union branch for a four-day week deal
Meet two colleagues to plan the co-op seriously

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loud and clear: the machines should belong to the workers, or at least be taxed hard enough to pay everyone's way. I'd be in the street if I had to. Two years isn't time to adjust, so the government has to step in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the thinking side of my job goes in 2028 and that doesn't bother me much. What bothers me is 2031, when robots could do the installs. I'd be thirty-two, and my skills would be worth a lot less unless I'm the one running the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the co-op within the year instead of in five. Pool savings with two or three guys, maybe twenty thousand between us plus a loan, and set it up to buy and run install robots as soon as they exist. I'd learn every AI tool going for design and quoting so the co-op runs lean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a sharp way. Like the start of a race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's a big risk with five months saved. What if the co-op fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go back to working for someone. Sam's nursing job is about as safe as anything in this picture, because people want a human holding their hand in hospital. That's our safety net, and I'd be honest with Sam about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the gap between the AI and the robots mean for your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three years between 2028 and 2031 are everything. That's when the office work is free and the hands still matter. A small co-op with no office costs could undercut the big contractors for three years and save enough to buy into the robots.

say: I'd say the machines should **belong to workers** or be taxed hard.
I'd protest if needed, because **two years** isn't time to adjust.
think: The **thinking side** going in 2028 barely bothers me.
By **2031** my install skills are worth less unless I run the robots.
do: Start the **co-op** within a year with two or three colleagues.
Pool about **twenty thousand** plus a loan to buy install robots later.
Learn every **AI tool** for design and quoting.
feel: **Anxious**, but sharp, like the start of a race.
S2.quote: A small co-op with no office costs could undercut the big contractors for three years and save enough to buy into the robots.
fieldNote: He treats the **three-year gap** as a business opportunity.
He relies on Sam's **nursing job** as the household safety net.
He's willing to risk **savings and a loan** that most of his peers wouldn't.

steps.text: Set up an electricians' co-op with two or three Voltway colleagues
Pool twenty thousand plus a bank loan for the co-op
Learn AI design and quoting tools to run the co-op lean
Join protests for worker ownership or taxing robot profits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to set this up properly, with worker-owned firms, training and a robot tax. I'd say it at the union and I'd write to my local representative about a co-op fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years to the AI and eight to the robots means I can be ready. I'd be thirty-five when the robots arrive, and I'd want to be running a business by then, not working for one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first two years planning the co-op properly: business course at the college, legal set-up, finding the right people. I'd keep working at Voltway and keep saving, aiming for ten months. Then launch around 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's coming, but I can see the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the older guys at Voltway who tease you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them there's a seat in the co-op for anyone who wants to learn. Some of them will laugh. But a few of them have twenty years of tricks that a robot would need someone to teach it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money and trust. Forty thousand is a lot, and going into business with friends can end friendships. I'd want a proper written agreement from day one.

say: I'd say we have time for **worker-owned firms** and a robot tax.
I'd write to my **local representative** about a co-op fund.
think: I can be **ready** with five years of warning.
I want to be **running a business** by thirty-five, not working for one.
do: Take a **business course** at the college in the first two years.
Save towards **ten months** of expenses while staying at Voltway.
feel: **Uneasy**, but he can see the road ahead.
S3.quote: A few of the older electricians have twenty years of tricks that a robot would need someone to teach it.
fieldNote: With more time he becomes a **careful planner** instead of a sprinter.
He worries about **money and trust** among co-op partners.
He sees the **older electricians'** experience as an asset, not a liability.

steps.text: Take a small business course at the college
Build savings to ten months while staying at Voltway
Write to the local representative asking for a co-op fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this right, and if we mess it up it's a political failure, not a technical one. I'd keep pushing for worker ownership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be forty when the robots arrive, with the co-op hopefully well established. Ten years is a whole career stage. I think I'd come out ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Voltway for two or three more years, build the co-op slowly, and start it when it's ready. I'd keep using AI tools daily, and I'd start learning robotics maintenance at the college once courses exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the extra time change your plans with Sam (your partner)?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably buy a place in a couple of years and think about kids later. With ten years, I'm not scared of signing a mortgage. Two years would have been different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to learn about robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to fix them and set them up on a site. If robots are wiring houses in 2039, someone has to keep them running. I'd like that someone to be an electrician, not a software firm two countries away.

say: I'd say ten years is enough, so failure would be **political**, not technical.
I'd keep pushing for **worker ownership** of the machines.
think: I'd be **forty** with the co-op hopefully well established.
Ten years is a whole career stage, and I'd **come out ahead**.
do: Stay at **Voltway** two or three more years while building the co-op.
Study **robotics maintenance** at the college once courses exist.
Buy a **place with Sam** in a couple of years.
S4.quote: If robots are wiring houses in 2039, someone has to keep them running.
fieldNote: A decade's warning makes him **hopeful** rather than anxious.
He wants **robot maintenance** to stay with local electricians.
His family plans, including a **mortgage**, go ahead with more time.

steps.text: Study robotics maintenance at the college once courses exist
Launch the co-op after two or three more years at Voltway
Buy a home with Sam within a couple of years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because I couldn't adapt, but because most people around me couldn't, and there'd be no support in place. What would help is a public fund that lets workers buy into automation together, so a crew of electricians could own the robots instead of a big contractor owning them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about who owns the machines. Everyone asks whether robots take jobs. The better question is whose robots they are. If workers own them, the same change could be good news.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks whether robots take jobs. The better question is whose robots they are, because if workers own them, the same change could be good news.
portrait: Rafael is a **27-year-old senior electrician** installing car chargers and shop fit-outs, and he uses AI every day.
He's **progressive** and thinks the real fight is over who owns the machines, not whether they arrive.
He's calm through AI Plateau and Steady Disruption, seeing AI as a **tool he already uses**.
In the AGI pictures he plans a **worker-owned co-op** that runs its own robots, and more time makes him calmer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because most of his colleagues and the government wouldn't be ready.
whatWouldHelp: A **public fund** that lets workers jointly buy and own automation.
